title: Introduction to FastAPI and Modern Web Services
subtitle: Build typed, validated, self-documenting web APIs in Python with FastAPI and Pydantic, from your first endpoint to a tested CRUD service with dependencies and interactive docs.
outcomes: Explain how ASGI servers such as Uvicorn run async Python web apps, and when to write async def or def endpoints
Create FastAPI applications with routers, path and query parameters, and the right HTTP methods and status codes
Validate requests and shape responses with Pydantic models, field constraints, validators and nested schemas
Share logic with dependencies for sessions, paging, lookups and API-key checks, and override them in tests
Document an API through its OpenAPI schema, and explore and test it in Swagger UI and ReDoc
prerequisites: Comfortable Python: functions, classes, dictionaries, modules, virtual environments and pip, as in Python Programming with PyCharm; type hints help but are explained here. A basic idea of HTTP requests, responses and status codes helps; Networking Fundamentals: How Networks and the Internet Work covers it. You need Python 3.10 or later, a terminal with curl, and a web browser.
description:
FastAPI has become a popular way to build web APIs in Python because it turns ordinary type hints into request parsing, validation and documentation. This course takes you from the ideas underneath, HTTP, ASGI and the event loop behind async and await, to a complete, tested CRUD service. You'll define routes with path and query parameters, return the right status codes and organise endpoints with routers; describe your data with Pydantic models, constraints, custom validators and nested schemas; share logic through FastAPI's dependency injection, from database sessions opened and closed for each request to API-key checks that tell 401 from 403; and make the generated OpenAPI documentation genuinely useful in Swagger UI and ReDoc.

Every module has a lab on one task API that grows from lab to lab, with starter files, TODOs to complete, and the exact output of each curl command and test run, all checked against current FastAPI. You'll even measure what blocking the event loop does. The capstone is a projects-and-tasks API you can use entirely from Swagger UI, with its own test suite.

modules.title: The Modern Web & ASGI
modules.summary: How Python web services work today: HTTP requests and responses, the move from WSGI to ASGI, the event loop behind async and await, and the type hints FastAPI is built on, ending with your first running API.

lessons.title: HTTP APIs, WSGI and ASGI
objectives: Describe what a web API receives and returns
Explain the difference between WSGI and ASGI, and what an ASGI server does
key_points: A web API receives HTTP requests, each with a method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE), a path, headers and sometimes a body, and returns a response with a status code, headers and usually a JSON body.

WSGI, the long-standing Python standard behind classic Flask and Django deployments, hands each request to the application as one synchronous call; ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is its asynchronous successor and also supports long-lived connections such as WebSockets.
In ASGI, the server handles the network and HTTP parsing, then calls the application, an async callable, with the request's details (the scope) and functions to receive and send messages.
FastAPI is built on Starlette, the ASGI toolkit that does the routing and responses, and on Pydantic, which does the data validation; an ASGI server such as Uvicorn runs it.
uvicorn main:app imports the object app from main.py and serves it, by default on http://127.0.0.1:8000; --reload restarts it whenever the code changes, which is for development only.

lessons.title: async and await in a web server
objectives: Explain how an event loop serves many requests at once
Choose between async def and def for a path operation
key_points: async def defines a coroutine function. Inside it, await pauses the coroutine until what it waits for, such as a network reply, is ready, and the event loop runs other coroutines in the meantime.
One process with an event loop can keep many requests in progress at once while they wait for I/O, such as a database, a file or another API; work that keeps the CPU busy doesn't benefit.
FastAPI runs a plain def path operation in a thread pool, so blocking code is safe there; an async def path operation runs on the event loop itself, so it must only await, never block.

A blocking call such as time.sleep() or requests.get() inside async def freezes the event loop and every other request with it; use await asyncio.sleep() and async clients such as httpx.AsyncClient instead.
asyncio.gather(first(), second()) runs awaitables concurrently, so two independent calls take about as long as the slower one rather than the sum of both.

lessons.title: Type hints and your first FastAPI app
objectives: Read the type hints FastAPI uses to parse and validate requests
Install FastAPI, run an app with the development server and find its documentation
key_points: Type hints such as def read_item(item_id: int, q: str | None = None) -> dict annotate parameters and return values. Python doesn't enforce them, but FastAPI reads them to parse, convert, validate and document each request.
Install with pip install "fastapi[standard]" in a virtual environment: it brings Uvicorn, the fastapi command and common extras. Current FastAPI needs Python 3.10 or later.
fastapi dev main.py starts a development server with auto-reload on http://127.0.0.1:8000; fastapi run main.py starts it for production, listening on 0.0.0.0 without reload.

app = FastAPI() creates the application, and a decorated function such as @app.get("/") def root(): return {"message": "Hello"} is a path operation; FastAPI turns the returned dict into a JSON response.
Interactive documentation appears by itself at /docs (Swagger UI) and /redoc (ReDoc), both generated from the OpenAPI schema served at /openapi.json.

files.content:
"""Send five requests at once to each /wait endpoint and time them: python timing.py"""
import asyncio
import time

import httpx

BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"


async def burst(client: httpx.AsyncClient, path: str, count: int = 5) -> float:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(client.get(path) for _ in range(count)))
    return time.perf_counter() - start


async def main() -> None:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=BASE_URL, timeout=30) as client:
        for path in ["/wait/sync", "/wait/async", "/wait/blocking"]:
            print(f"{path:<15} 5 requests in {await burst(client, path):.1f} s")


asyncio.run(main())

hints: If fastapi isn't found, activate the virtual environment in that terminal.
Port 8000 in use? Start with fastapi dev main.py --port 8001 and change BASE_URL in timing.py to match.
Timings vary by a tenth of a second or so; the pattern is what matters.
/wait/sync is a plain def, so FastAPI runs each request in its thread pool.

modules.title: FastAPI Fundamentals & Routing
modules.summary: Set up a FastAPI project and define its routes: path operations for each HTTP method, path and query parameters with validation, status codes and errors, and APIRouter to keep a growing API organised.

lessons.title: Path operations and HTTP methods
objectives: Map HTTP methods and paths to Python functions
Choose the right method and status code for each operation
key_points: A path operation joins an HTTP method and a path to a function: @app.get reads, @app.post creates, @app.put replaces, @app.patch changes part of a resource and @app.delete removes it.
REST APIs name resources with nouns and let the method say what happens: GET /tasks lists tasks, POST /tasks creates one, GET /tasks/{task_id} reads one and DELETE /tasks/{task_id} deletes it.

Status codes tell the client what happened: 200 OK, 201 Created (status_code=201 on the decorator), 204 No Content, 400 for a bad request, 401 and 403 for authentication and permission, 404 Not Found, 422 for invalid input and 500 for a server error.
raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Task not found") stops the request and sends a JSON error body: {"detail": "Task not found"}.
Routes are matched in the order they're declared, so a fixed path such as /tasks/summary must come before /tasks/{task_id}, or summary is taken for an ID and rejected with a 422.

lessons.title: Path and query parameters
objectives: Declare path and query parameters with types and defaults
Validate parameters with Query and Path
key_points: A path parameter is part of the URL, named in both the path and the function: @app.get("/tasks/{task_id}") def read(task_id: int). FastAPI converts "42" to 42 and answers 422 for a value that isn't a number.
Function parameters that aren't in the path are query parameters: def list_tasks(limit: int = 10, offset: int = 0) reads /tasks?limit=10&offset=20, and a parameter without a default is required.
None as a default makes a query parameter optional, as in done: bool | None = None; for booleans FastAPI accepts true and false, 1 and 0, yes and no, and on and off.

Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] adds validation and documentation to a query parameter, and Annotated[int, Path(ge=1)] to a path parameter; a value out of range gets a 422 that names the parameter.
An Enum or a Literal type limits a parameter to a list of values, which the docs offer as a choice.

lessons.title: Responses, status codes and routers
objectives: Control what a path operation returns and with which status
Organise routes into modules with APIRouter
key_points: FastAPI converts what you return, such as dicts, lists, Pydantic models and dates, to JSON and sends it with Content-Type: application/json.
A return type annotation or response_model makes FastAPI check and filter the response against that type; when it's a Pydantic model, recent versions also serialise it with Pydantic's fast core.
status_code=204 on the decorator sends an empty body; returning a Response (or JSONResponse) directly gives full control of the status, headers and body.
APIRouter groups related routes in their own module: router = APIRouter(prefix="/tasks", tags=["tasks"]) in app/routers/tasks.py, then app.include_router(router) in app/main.py.
When only /tasks exists, a request for /tasks/ is redirected with a 307 to /tasks, so clients should use paths exactly as documented.

name = "task-api"

requires-python = ">=3.10"

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]

"""The task API."""

"""The tasks the API serves, kept in memory for now."""

SEED = [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Write the release notes", "done": False, "priority": 2},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Review the API design", "done": True, "priority": 1},
    {"id": 3, "title": "Fix the login bug", "done": False, "priority": 1},
    {"id": 4, "title": "Update the dependencies", "done": False, "priority": 3},
]

TASKS: dict[int, dict] = {}


def reset() -> None:
    """Put the tasks back to the seed data. The tests call this before each test."""
    TASKS.clear()
    TASKS.update({task["id"]: dict(task) for task in SEED})


reset()
"""One module per group of endpoints."""

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import APIRouter, HTTPException, Path, Query

from app.data import TASKS

router = APIRouter(prefix="/tasks", tags=["tasks"])


@router.get("")
def list_tasks(
    done: bool | None = None,
    priority: Annotated[int | None, Query(ge=1, le=3)] = None,
    limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10,
    offset: Annotated[int, Query(ge=0)] = 0,
) -> list[dict]:
    """List tasks, optionally only done or open ones, or only one priority."""
    # TODO 1: keep the tasks in TASKS.values() that match done and priority (a filter that is None
    #        matches everything), then return the slice that offset and limit describe
    return list(TASKS.values())


# TODO 2: add GET /tasks/summary, returning {"total": number of tasks, "done": number done}.
#        Declare it here, before /{task_id}, or "summary" would be taken for a task ID.


@router.get("/{task_id}")
def read_task(task_id: Annotated[int, Path(ge=1)]) -> dict:
    """One task, by its ID."""
    if task_id not in TASKS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Task not found")
    return TASKS[task_id]


# TODO 3: add DELETE /tasks/{task_id}: remove the task and answer 204 No Content, or raise a 404
#        with the detail "Task not found" if there's no such task

hints: A task matches when each filter is None or equal to the task's value.
fastapi dev reloads when you save, so there's no need to restart it.
The autouse fixture calls data.reset() before each test, so a deletion in one test doesn't affect the next.
status_code=204 on the decorator, with a function that returns None, gives an empty response.

modules.title: Data Validation with Pydantic
modules.summary: Define the shape of the data your API accepts and returns with Pydantic: request bodies validated automatically, constraints and custom validators, clear 422 errors, nested models, and response models that never leak internal fields.

lessons.title: Pydantic models and request bodies
objectives: Declare request bodies with Pydantic models
Separate what clients send from what the API returns
key_points: A Pydantic model is a class of typed fields, as in class TaskCreate(BaseModel): title: str; priority: int = 2. A path operation parameter typed with a model is read from the JSON request body.
FastAPI parses the body, validates it against the model and passes your function a model instance; model_dump() turns it back into a dict.
In its default lax mode Pydantic converts compatible values, such as "3" to 3 for an int field, and rejects values it can't convert; strict=True on a field or in model_config turns conversion off.

Send JSON bodies with a JSON Content-Type such as application/json: recent FastAPI versions don't read the body as JSON otherwise. With curl, add -H "Content-Type: application/json" (curl 7.82 and later also have --json).
Use separate models for what clients send and what they get back: TaskCreate to create, TaskUpdate with optional fields for PATCH, and Task, with the server-owned id and done, for responses.

lessons.title: Field constraints and validation errors
objectives: Constrain fields with Field and standard types
Read and produce clear validation errors, including your own
key_points: Field() adds constraints: min_length and max_length for strings and lists, ge, gt, le and lt for numbers, and pattern for a regular expression; Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1)] makes a constrained type you can reuse.
Standard types validate formats: date and datetime (ISO 8601 strings), UUID, HttpUrl, Literal["low", "high"] for fixed values, and EmailStr, which needs the email-validator package.

A failed validation returns 422 with a detail list, one entry per problem, each with a type (such as string_too_short), a loc (such as ["body", "title"]), a msg and the input, so a client can fix everything at once.

@field_validator("title") on a classmethod checks or cleans one field, such as stripping spaces and rejecting blanks; @model_validator(mode="after") checks rules across fields. Raising ValueError gives a value_error entry.
model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") rejects unknown fields, so a misspelt "titel" is an error instead of being silently ignored.

lessons.title: Nested models and response models
objectives: Validate nested data with models inside models
Shape responses and partial updates with response models and exclude_unset
key_points: Models can contain models and lists of them, as in checklist: list[ChecklistItem] = []. Nested data is validated all the way down, and an error's loc points at the item, such as ["body", "checklist", 0, "text"].
A response model filters what goes out: return a TaskInDB with an internal created_by field from a path operation declared to return Task, and created_by is never sent.
For partial updates, model_dump(exclude_unset=True) gives only the fields the client actually sent, and model_copy(update=...) applies them to the stored object.
Mutable defaults such as [] are safe for Pydantic fields, because each instance gets its own copy, unlike default values in Python functions.
Field(examples=[...]) and model_config's json_schema_extra add examples that appear in the generated documentation.

[project]
name = "task-api"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = ["fastapi[standard]"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]
testpaths = ["tests"]
"""The task API."""

from datetime import date
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, field_validator

Title = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=200, examples=["Write the release notes"])]
Priority = Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=3, description="1 is the most urgent, 3 the least")]


def clean_title(value: str | None) -> str | None:
    if value is not None:
        value = value.strip()
        if not value:
            raise ValueError("title can't be blank")
    return value


class ChecklistItem(BaseModel):
    text: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)]
    done: bool = False


class TaskCreate(BaseModel):
    """What a client sends to create or replace a task."""

    # TODO 1: reject unknown fields, such as a misspelt "titel", with model_config = ConfigDict(...)

    title: Title
    # TODO 2: add priority (a Priority, default 2), due (a date or None, default None) and
    #        checklist (a list of ChecklistItem, default an empty list)

    # TODO 3: add a field validator for title that strips spaces and rejects a blank title
    #        (call clean_title)


class TaskUpdate(BaseModel):
    """A partial update: send only the fields to change."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")

    title: Title | None = None
    priority: Priority | None = None
    due: date | None = None
    done: bool | None = None

    @field_validator("title")
    @classmethod
    def title_is_not_blank(cls, value: str | None) -> str | None:
        return clean_title(value)


class Task(TaskCreate):
    """A task as the API returns it."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="ignore")

    id: int
    done: bool = False


class TaskInDB(Task):
    """What the server stores: also who created the task, which the API never returns."""

    created_by: str = "seed"

"""The tasks the API serves, kept in memory for now, as TaskInDB models."""

from app.models import TaskInDB

SEED = [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Write the release notes", "priority": 2, "due": "2025-07-01"},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Review the API design", "priority": 1, "done": True},
    {"id": 3, "title": "Fix the login bug", "priority": 1,
     "checklist": [{"text": "Reproduce it", "done": True}, {"text": "Write a test"}]},
    {"id": 4, "title": "Update the dependencies", "priority": 3},
]

TASKS: dict[int, TaskInDB] = {}
_next_id = 1


def reset() -> None:
    """Put the tasks back to the seed data. The tests call this before each test."""
    global _next_id
    TASKS.clear()
    for item in SEED:
        TASKS[item["id"]] = TaskInDB(**item)
    _next_id = max(TASKS) + 1


def new_id() -> int:
    global _next_id
    _next_id += 1
    return _next_id - 1


reset()
"""One module per group of endpoints."""

hints: Field constraints run before your field_validator, so an empty title fails min_length and "   " reaches clean_title.
task.model_dump() gives the validated fields as a dict, ready to pass to TaskInDB(...) with ** .
exclude_unset=True leaves out fields the client didn't send, even ones with defaults.
If curl answers with model_attributes_type, the Content-Type header is missing.

modules.title: Dependency Injection System
modules.summary: FastAPI's dependency injection: reusable functions and classes the framework calls for you, chains of dependencies, set-up and clean-up with yield for database sessions, and dependencies that enforce security and can be swapped in tests.

lessons.title: Dependencies with Depends()
objectives: Declare and reuse dependencies with Depends and Annotated
Explain how FastAPI calls dependencies and caches their results
key_points: A dependency is a function, or another callable, that a path operation declares as a parameter with Depends(), as in page: Annotated[Page, Depends(pagination)]; FastAPI calls it first and passes in the result.
Dependencies take the same kinds of parameters as path operations, query, path, header and body, with the same validation, and those parameters appear in the docs.
Dependencies remove repetition: paging, filters, the current user, settings or a database session are written once and reused by every endpoint that needs them.
An Annotated alias such as PageDep = Annotated[Page, Depends(pagination)] makes reuse tidy: def list_tasks(page: PageDep).
Within one request, a dependency used in several places is called once and its result shared; Depends(dependency, use_cache=False) asks for a fresh call each time.

lessons.title: Sub-dependencies, classes and yield
objectives: Build chains of dependencies, including classes
Manage resources such as database sessions with yield dependencies
key_points: Dependencies can depend on other dependencies, forming a graph FastAPI resolves for you, such as writer depending on current_user, which depends on the API-key header.
A class works as a dependency too: Depends(Paginator) calls the class with the request's parameters and passes in the instance.

A dependency that yields does set-up before the request and clean-up after: session = Session(); try: yield session; finally: session.close(). The clean-up runs after the response is sent, or as soon as the endpoint returns with Depends(get_session, scope="function").
An exception raised in the endpoint reaches the dependency at its yield, so it can roll back; a dependency that catches an exception should raise it again, or the error is hidden.
FastAPI solves dependencies in order, those in the decorator's dependencies= first. An HTTPException in one stops the request, so check authentication before dependencies that open resources.

lessons.title: Dependencies for security and shared resources
objectives: Protect operations with security dependencies that tell 401 from 403
Swap dependencies in tests with dependency_overrides
key_points: dependencies=[Depends(writer)] on a decorator runs a check without passing its result to the function; the same list on APIRouter(...) or FastAPI(...) applies it to every route there.
A security dependency stops the request by raising HTTPException: 401 when credentials are missing or wrong (with a WWW-Authenticate header), and 403 when they're valid but not allowed.
APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key", auto_error=False) from fastapi.security reads the key and declares the scheme in the OpenAPI schema, which adds the Authorize button to Swagger UI.
A session or repository dependency keeps endpoints unaware of storage, so the same code can run against an in-memory store, SQLite or a database server.
app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = fake_session replaces a dependency for tests without touching the endpoints; clear the overrides after each test.

files.content:
[project]
name = "task-api"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = ["fastapi[standard]"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["."]
testpaths = ["tests"]

from app.db import Session, Store
from app.dependencies import ApiUser, writer
from app.main import app
from tests.conftest import READER, WRITER


def test_pagination_is_shared_and_validated(client):
    assert [t["id"] for t in client.get("/tasks?limit=2&offset=1").json()] == [2, 3]
    assert client.get("/tasks?limit=0").status_code == 422


def test_reading_needs_no_key_but_writing_does(client):
    assert client.get("/tasks/1").status_code == 200
    response = client.post("/tasks", json={"title": "Plan the sprint"})
    assert response.status_code == 401
    assert response.headers["www-authenticate"] == "ApiKey"


def test_a_read_only_key_is_forbidden_to_write(client):
    response = client.delete("/tasks/1", headers=READER)
    assert response.status_code == 403
    assert response.json() == {"detail": "This API key can't change tasks"}


def test_a_writer_can_create_and_delete(client):
    created = client.post("/tasks", json={"title": "Plan the sprint"}, headers=WRITER)
    assert created.status_code == 201
    assert client.delete(f"/tasks/{created.json()['id']}", headers=WRITER).status_code == 204


def test_missing_tasks_are_404_before_any_change(client):
    assert client.patch("/tasks/99", json={"done": True}, headers=WRITER).status_code == 404


def test_every_session_is_closed_even_after_an_error(client):
    before = Session.opened
    client.get("/tasks")
    client.get("/tasks/99")
    assert Session.opened == before + 2
    assert Session.open_now == 0


# TODO 4: use app.dependency_overrides to replace writer with a function returning
#        ApiUser("test@example.com", can_write=True), then check POST /tasks works without any key


def test_overriding_the_session_gives_a_private_store(client):
    from app.db import get_session

    private = Store()
    private.tasks.clear()

    def private_session():
        session = Session(private)
        yield session
        session.close()

    app.dependency_overrides[get_session] = private_session
    assert client.get("/tasks").json() == []
"""The task API."""
"""One module per group of endpoints."""

hints: Put session.close() in a finally block, so it runs even when the endpoint raises.
Dependencies are solved in parameter order: create_task asks for the writer before the session.
app.dependency_overrides is keyed by the original function, so import writer from app.dependencies.
The conftest fixture clears the overrides after every test.

modules.title: Interactive API Documentation
modules.summary: The documentation FastAPI generates from your code: the OpenAPI schema, Swagger UI for trying requests and ReDoc for reading, and the metadata, tags, error responses and examples that make them useful to the people who call your API.

lessons.title: OpenAPI: the schema behind the docs
objectives: Explain what the OpenAPI schema contains and how FastAPI builds it
Set an API's metadata and export its schema
key_points: OpenAPI is a standard, language-independent description of an HTTP API: its paths, operations, parameters, request and response bodies and security schemes. FastAPI generates it from your code and serves it at /openapi.json.
Pydantic models become JSON Schemas under components/schemas, and every operation refers to them, so the documentation can't drift away from the code.
Tools read the schema: client generators produce typed clients in many languages, API gateways and testing tools import it, and Swagger UI and ReDoc render it.
FastAPI(title=..., version=..., summary=..., description=...) sets the API's metadata, with the description in Markdown; summary= and the function's docstring describe each operation.
app.openapi() returns the schema as a dict, so a short script can save it as openapi.json for review and versioning.

lessons.title: Swagger UI and ReDoc
objectives: Try an API's operations in Swagger UI, with credentials
Choose between Swagger UI and ReDoc, and turn them off when needed
key_points: /docs serves Swagger UI: expand an operation, choose Try it out, fill in its parameters or body and choose Execute to send a real request and see the curl command, the response code, headers and body.
When the API declares security schemes, Swagger UI shows an Authorize button and a lock on each protected operation; the credentials you enter go with every request you try.
/redoc serves ReDoc, a three-panel, read-only reference that suits the people who use your API; both read the same /openapi.json.
docs_url=None, redoc_url=None or openapi_url=None turns them off, for example for a private production service, and include_in_schema=False hides one route.
Swagger UI sends real requests, so point it at a development or test server, never at production data you can't afford to change.

lessons.title: Making the docs useful
objectives: Organise and describe operations with tags, summaries and documented errors
Keep the schema stable as a contract with your API's users
key_points: Tags group operations, and openapi_tags= on FastAPI() gives each tag a description and sets their order.
responses={404: {"model": Message, "description": "No task has this ID"}} documents an error an operation can return, beyond the success response and the 422 FastAPI adds itself.
deprecated=True marks an operation as deprecated, shown struck through in Swagger UI, so clients can move away from it before it's removed.
Examples on fields, such as Field(examples=["Write the release notes"]), fill in Try it out's request body and show readers what valid data looks like.
Version the API with a prefix such as /v1 and the version in FastAPI(), and treat openapi.json as a contract: commit it and review its diff, so a breaking change is noticed before clients find it.

files.content:
import logging

from fastapi import FastAPI

from app.routers import tasks

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")

DESCRIPTION = """
Keep track of tasks: create them, list and filter them, update them and tick them off.

Reading is open to everyone. Changing tasks needs an **X-API-Key** header: in Swagger UI,
choose **Authorize** and enter `dev-writer-key`.
"""

app = FastAPI(
    title="Task API",
    version="1.0.0",
    summary="A small task management service.",
    description=DESCRIPTION,
    # TODO 1: describe the two tags with openapi_tags: "tasks" (Create, read, update and delete
    #        tasks.) and "service" (Health checks.)
)
app.include_router(tasks.router)


@app.get("/health", tags=["service"], summary="Check that the service is up")
def health() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": "ok"}

"""Write the API's OpenAPI schema to openapi.json and summarise it: python export_openapi.py"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

from app.main import app

schema = app.openapi()
Path("openapi.json").write_text(json.dumps(schema, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")

print(f"{schema['info']['title']} {schema['info']['version']} (OpenAPI {schema['openapi']})")
for path, operations in schema["paths"].items():
    for method, operation in operations.items():
        note = "  (deprecated)" if operation.get("deprecated") else ""
        print(f"{method.upper():<7}{path:<18}{operation.get('summary', '')}{note}")
schemas = schema["components"]["schemas"]
print(f"{len(schemas)} schemas: {', '.join(sorted(schemas))}")
print("security schemes:", ", ".join(schema["components"].get("securitySchemes", {})))

def test_the_schema_describes_the_api(client):
    schema = client.get("/openapi.json").json()
    assert schema["info"]["title"] == "Task API"
    assert [tag["name"] for tag in schema["tags"]] == ["tasks", "service"]
    assert "404" in schema["paths"]["/tasks/{task_id}"]["get"]["responses"]
    assert schema["paths"]["/tasks/open/all"]["get"]["deprecated"] is True


def test_the_docs_pages_are_served(client):
    assert "swagger-ui" in client.get("/docs").text
    assert "redoc" in client.get("/redoc").text


def test_the_example_title_appears_in_the_schema(client):
    schema = client.get("/openapi.json").json()
    title = schema["components"]["schemas"]["TaskCreate"]["properties"]["title"]
    assert title["examples"] == ["Write the release notes"]

hints: openapi_tags is a list of dicts with name and description keys, in the order the docs should show them.
FastAPI caches the schema after the first call; restart the server to see changes in /docs.
If Authorize doesn't appear, check that the routes still use the writer dependency built on APIKeyHeader.

study_plan.focus: HTTP, ASGI and async, your first FastAPI app, then routes with path and query parameters; finish both labs.
Validate requests and shape responses with Pydantic models; finish the validation lab.
Dependency injection for sessions, paging and security, then the interactive documentation.
Build and test the task management capstone, then review with the mock exam and flashcards.

project.title: A task management API
project.brief: Build a complete RESTful API for a small team's task manager with FastAPI, building on the labs. It has projects and tasks: every task belongs to a project, so tasks live under /projects/{project_id}/tasks. Provide CRUD operations for both, with the right methods and status codes (201 with the new resource, 204 for deletions, 404 for anything that doesn't exist, 409 for a project name that's taken). Validate everything with Pydantic: separate create, update and response models, constraints, a custom validator, a nested checklist, unknown fields rejected, and an internal field that's never returned. Use dependency injection for a simulated database session opened and closed for each request, for paging and filters, for finding a project or task or answering 404, and for API keys with read and write access. Document the API so that someone else could use it entirely from Swagger UI: metadata, tags, summaries, examples and documented errors. Test it with TestClient, including dependency overrides, and export openapi.json.
deliverables: The source code, organised in modules (main, models, db, dependencies and one router per resource)
At least fifteen pytest tests using TestClient, covering success and error cases and at least one dependency override, all passing
A README with how to install and run the API, the demo keys, and a short tour of the endpoints
A transcript or screenshots of a full session in Swagger UI: create a project, add tasks, update one, list with filters, delete, and the errors for a missing key and a missing task

rubric.name: REST design and CRUD
rubric.description: Projects and tasks are complete and consistent: nested paths, the right methods, 201, 204, 404 and 409 where they belong, and errors in one shape.

rubric.name: Validation and models
rubric.description: Separate create, update and response models; constraints, a custom validator and a nested model; unknown fields rejected; the internal field never returned; partial updates with exclude_unset.

rubric.name: Dependency injection
rubric.description: Sessions opened and closed with yield; shared paging and filters; lookup dependencies for 404s; API keys that distinguish 401 from 403; nothing duplicated across routes.

rubric.name: Documentation
rubric.description: The whole API can be used from Swagger UI: metadata, tag descriptions, summaries, examples, documented errors and working Authorize.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: At least fifteen meaningful tests, independent of each other, including error paths and a dependency override.

rubric.name: Code organisation and README
rubric.description: Clear modules and names, and a README another developer could follow.

project.submit: Paste your code (each file with its name) or a repository link, your tests with the pytest summary, the first lines of openapi.json and the output of a script like export_openapi.py, your README, and the Swagger UI transcript or screenshots.
